Worked examples · downloadable · copy-paste

The Deterministic Classifier Lab

How to classify free-text complaints so that five people running the same thing get exactly the same answer, and how to prove it. Keyword rules, a frozen TF-IDF + logistic regression model, and Python in Excel code you can paste straight in.

Takeaways1 Ladder2 Try it3 Download4 Python in Excel 5 Final output6 Numbers7 Seed test8 Same vs different9 Freezing10 Conclusion11 Fuzzy lookup?12 Formulas only13 Why Python14 Make the case

The seven takeaways

  1. You can freeze a TF-IDF classifier so the same 900 complaints get the same 900 labels every time. Fix the data and the split seed, record the fingerprint, then paste the labels as values. Five retrains matched exactly, on two different library versions.
  2. Take the seed out and the answer moves. A seedless run labelled 32 of the 900 complaints differently, and a second seedless run disagreed with the first on 48.
  3. The movement sits where the model was unsure. Keyword-rule labels never changed. Of the 604 complaints the model decided, 32 (5.3%) changed, and 96.9% of all changes were on complaints it was under 80% confident about.
  4. Reproducible is not the same as correct. The model is right on 85.6% of complaints it hasn't seen. Freezing makes the errors repeatable, so they can be found and fixed.
  5. A scored keyword lookup and a trained classifier are close cousins. Both add up word evidence. The difference is who writes the list: a person, or training on labelled examples. Fuzzy spelling hardly helped on our test, because the missing words weren't misspelt, they were unlisted. Section 11 shows the numbers.
  6. A frozen model is just a table of weights, and a table runs as plain formulas. Exported to a sheet, the learned weights score 85.6% on held-out complaints using only SUMPRODUCT and SEARCH, the same accuracy as the Python model. What gives the same answer every time is the fixed table, not a clever algorithm and not the seed. Section 12 has the formulas and a downloadable workbook, and section 13 sets out why Python is still worth using.
  7. None of this measures Copilot. It shows what can be pinned. Section 14 gives you a test to measure Copilot on the same yardstick, and it could go either way.

1The reproducibility ladder

"Deterministic" means the same input always gives the same output. Three common ways to classify text sit at very different points on that scale.

DeterministicKeyword and scoring rules
  • Same text + same table version = same label
  • Every label points to the words that caused it
  • Only recognises wording you anticipated
Reproducible once frozenTrained classifier
  • TF-IDF + logistic regression, fixed seed, saved model
  • Same input + same model version = same label
  • Less explainable; accuracy must be measured
Not guaranteedLLM prompt
  • "Classify this against my table"
  • Can differ between runs, users and model updates
  • Microsoft's own docs say generative answers aren't deterministic
The design rule used on this pageAn AI may help you build the keyword table or write the code. Whatever runs on your complaints must be rules or a frozen model, so a re-run gives the same result and every label records which version produced it.

2Try it

Two demos. The first is the real rules engine from the Python code below, running in your browser. The second is an illustration of why a sampling model varies.

A · Rules scorer (real, deterministic)

Rule: a category needs a score of at least 3 and a lead of at least 2 over the runner-up, otherwise the complaint is left unclassified for a model or a person. Ties break by a fixed priority order.

B · Sampling illustration (made-up probabilities)

Imagine a model gives these probabilities for one borderline complaint. These numbers are invented for illustration; this is not a real model. A generative model samples from such a distribution, so repeat runs can land on different labels. Move temperature down and the pick becomes more stable, but in real LLMs even temperature 0 isn't a guarantee.

4Worked example in Python in Excel

Seventeen cells, run in order. Each has a copy button and the real output from my test run.

Set up the workbook

  1. Download the two CSVs above. In Excel use Data → From Text/CSV to load each onto its own sheet.
  2. Click inside each dataset, press Ctrl+T to make it a table, then rename the tables on the Table Design tab: Complaints and Rules.
  3. On a new sheet, click a cell, then Formulas → Insert Python (or type =PY(), paste cell 1, and press Ctrl+Enter.
  4. Paste each next cell into the next cell below. Python in Excel runs cells row by row, top to bottom, so order matters and later cells reuse earlier variables.
  5. For cells that return a table, set the output to Excel Value to see the grid. Cells 9 and 11 return all 900 rows, so keep the space below and to the right of them empty.
  6. Cells 14 and 15 compare two runs and need a second Table called Runs with columns complaint_id, run_1, run_2. Sections 9 and 11 explain how to fill it.
Before using real complaintsPython in Excel runs calculations in Microsoft's cloud. Check with your information security or data protection team that your real complaint data is allowed there. Practise with this synthetic data first.

5The final output: all 900 complaints

Cell 9 labels every complaint and keeps both methods side by side, so you can see exactly where they differ. This is the table you would hand to someone.

The same table cell 9 returns in Excel

All 900 rows are below. Search them, filter them, or show every row at once. Filter used_for to test to see only the complaints the model had never seen.

What each column means
true_label
The known right answer. It only exists because this data is synthetic; with real complaints this is your hand-labelled sample.
rule_label, rule_matched
What the keyword rules decided (blank if they were not confident) and the exact words that triggered it.
model_label, model_confidence
The TF-IDF model's best guess for every complaint, and the probability it assigns to that guess.
final_label, final_method
The decision: rules first; otherwise the model if it is at least 60% confident; otherwise "Needs review" for a person.
used_for
train = the model learned from this complaint. test = the model never saw it.
correct
final_label equals true_label. "Needs review" counts as not correct, because nothing has been decided yet.
version
Which rules table and model version produced the label.
Read used_for before you quote any accuracy720 of the 900 complaints were used to teach the model. On those it gets 98.8% right, because it has effectively seen the answers. On the 180 it had never seen it gets 85.6%. Only the second number tells you how it will do on new complaints, in the same way a student's score on the practice paper they revised from says little about the real exam. (Both figures are the model's own labels, before the review queue.)

Run through the full pipeline, the 180 test complaints came out like this: 165 were labelled automatically and 89.1% of those were right (147 of 165), and 15 were sent to a person.

Rules versus TF-IDF: what is actually different in the output

Keyword rulesTF-IDF + logistic regression
Gives a label forOnly the complaints where a strong, clear match exists (64 of the 180 test complaints)Every complaint: it always has a best guess plus a confidence
Accuracy where it speaks82.8% (on the complaints it labelled)89.1% on those same complaints; 85.6% across all 180
Why did it choose that?You can read the exact words that matchedIt learned word weights from examples. It can't give you a single reason you could write on a file.
Unfamiliar wordingNo match, so no labelGuesses from similar words; low confidence goes to review
What changes the outputEditing the keyword tableChanging the training data, the settings or the train/test split

When the two methods disagree

On the 64 test complaints where the rules fired, the model gave the same label on 50. On the other 14 they disagreed: the model was right 9 times, the rules 5 times, and neither was right 0 times. Four real examples:

ComplaintTrue labelRules saidModel saidWho was right
I have been a customer for years. The webchat agent ended the conversation without solving anything. Also, i have been billed an annual fee I never agreed to. I expect compensation.Customer ServiceFees & Charges
(fee, billed)		Customer Service
(68% confident)		Model
The costs keep creeping up and my balance is lower than it should be. Also, the staff member was rude and dismissive when I called.Fees & ChargesCustomer Service
(rude, staff)		Fees & Charges
(51% confident)		Model
To whom it may concern, I was misled about what the insurance actually included. Also, your advisor gave me different answers on two separate calls. I expect compensation.Mis-sellingMis-selling
(misled, insurance)		Customer Service
(60% confident)		Rules
This is the second time I have raised this. The password reset keeps failing and I am locked out. Also, the terms were very different from what I was promised at the time of sale.Account AccessAccount Access
(locked, password, reset)		Mis-selling
(65% confident)		Rules
Why these disagreements are mostly two-issue complaintsIn this synthetic data the "true" label is the first issue mentioned. Keyword counting can't know which issue comes first or matters most. Real complaints have the same problem, so decide in advance what counts as the main issue, or let a person decide whenever a complaint mentions two categories.

Why the pipeline puts rules first anyway. Rules can show their working. In this run the model was more accurate than the rules on the same complaints (89.1% against 82.8%), so rules-first buys explainability at some cost in accuracy. You could reverse the order, or accept a label only when both agree and send everything else to review. That is a policy choice, not a technical one.

6Reading the numbers

What the figures in cells 2, 5 and 6 mean, with the real numbers from this run.

Train 720, test 180

There are 900 complaints, 150 in each of the 6 categories. Cell 2 sets aside 20% (180) and keeps 80% (720).

  • Train (720): the complaints the model learns from. Think of them as the revision notes.
  • Test (180): complaints locked away until the end. The model has never seen them, so scoring it on them is a fair exam.
  • Why it matters: any model can look brilliant on data it has already learned. The test score is the only one that predicts real-world performance.
  • Why 30 per category: the split is "stratified", so each category gets exactly 30 of the 180 test places. No category is accidentally missing from the exam.
  • What the seed does: it decides which 180 complaints are held back. The same seed gives the same 180 every time.

Precision, recall, F1 and support

Cell 5 produces one row per category. Here is what each column means, using the Fraud & Scams row as the worked example.

Support (30)
How many real Fraud & Scams complaints were in the test set. It tells you how many examples each row is based on. Here it is 30 for every category, so the rows are equally trustworthy.
Precision (0.92)
"When the model says Fraud, how often is it right?" It labelled 25 complaints as fraud and 23 really were: 23 / 25 = 0.92. Low precision means a pile of wrongly flagged complaints.
Recall (0.77)
"Of the real fraud complaints, how many did it find?" There were 30 and it found 23: 23 / 30 = 0.77. The 7 it missed were labelled Account Access (3), Delays & Processing (2), Mis-selling (2). Low recall means real cases slipping through.
F1 (0.84)
A single score that combines precision and recall (their harmonic mean). It sits closer to the lower of the two, so you can't hide poor recall behind good precision.
Accuracy (85.6%)
The simplest one: 154 correct out of 180.
Macro and weighted average
The average across the six categories. They are identical here because every category has the same support. With uneven categories they would differ.

Which matters more? It depends on the cost of a mistake. For fraud you probably care most about recall (don't miss real cases). For a team with limited review time you may care more about precision (don't flood them with false alarms).

What the five runs mean

Cell 6 trains the model from scratch five times and computes a fingerprint: a short code that summarises every prediction and every probability for all 900 complaints. If any single label or probability differed, the code would change.

  • What it shows: five fresh trainings on the same 720 complaints with the same settings gave identical results. Nothing in training or prediction is random.
  • What it doesn't show: that the model is accurate, that it would match after you change the data or the split (experiment B below does exactly that), or that it matches on every machine. It matched across the two library versions I tested, but other versions could differ, so record the fingerprint alongside the version.

All 900 complaints, without the seed

Cell 11 is the seedless version of cell 9: the same pipeline and the same 900 complaints, retrained with no seed on the split. It sits next to the seeded labels so every change is visible. The table below is one run of it. 32 of the 900 final labels differ from the seeded run. I then ran cell 11 a second time with nothing changed, and 48 labels differed from the first seedless run.

Your own run in Excel will give a different table

Filter changed_vs_seeded to True to see only the complaints whose label moved. Rows highlighted in amber are the ones that changed.

  • Neither run is "the" right one. Of the 32 complaints whose label changed, the seeded run was right on 20 and the seedless run on 11. The point is that they disagree about the same complaints.
  • The flips happen on borderline complaints. In the seeded run, the complaints that later changed had an average model confidence of 68%, against 88% for the ones that never changed.
  • Rule-labelled complaints never change. The keyword rules don't depend on the split, so every flip comes from the model.

What the summary experiment shows

  • A. Seed 42 everywhere: one fingerprint, the same accuracy and zero differences, five times out of five.
  • B. No seed on the split: 5 different fingerprints in 5 runs. Test accuracy ranged from 83.3% to 86.7%, and between 47 and 55 of the 900 complaints received a different label from the baseline.
  • C. No seed on the classifier only: nothing changed at all. With scikit-learn's default solver, logistic regression has no random step, so the seed in cell 4 was harmless insurance and not what made the result repeatable. I'd assumed it mattered; the experiment says otherwise.
  • D. No seeds at all: 5 different fingerprints in 5 runs, the same behaviour as B.

Why leaving out the split seed changes the answer

Without a seed, each run picks a different random 180 complaints to hold back. The model then learns from a different 720, so its word weights shift slightly, and complaints sitting on the border between two categories tip the other way. The accuracy also moves partly because each run is marked on a different exam paper. Quote the seed whenever you quote an accuracy figure.

The important distinctionHere the variation comes from a choice you made (a random split), and you can switch it off with a seed. Once the split is fixed, the model gives the same answer every time. With an LLM prompt there is no equivalent dial in your hands: the randomness sits inside the model and its serving infrastructure, so you can't pin it from your side.

What it shows

  • Rule-labelled complaints never change. 296 out of 296 matched, by construction.
  • Confident model decisions are stable. Among complaints the seeded model was 90% or more sure about, 0 of 371 changed. At 80 to 90%, 1 of 98 changed.
  • The movement sits where the model was unsure. At 60 to 80% confidence, 25 of 89 changed. Among complaints that were already sent to review (under 60%), 6 of 46 changed. Overall, 96.9% of all the changes were on complaints the seeded model was under 80% confident about.
  • Many differences are about the review line, not the category. Of the 32 changes, 19 were a complaint moving into or out of "Needs review" (the model crossing the 60% confidence line), and 13 were a real swap from one category to another. The first kind is less harmful, because a person looks at it anyway. The second kind is a confident label that moved.
What this means for "same result every time"With the seed pinned, all 900 labels are identical on every run. Without it, a small and predictable group of borderline complaints move, and a second unseeded run moved a different small group (48 labels differed from the first). The size is modest. The important part is that nothing tells you in advance which complaints will move unless the seed is fixed.

9Freezing it in place

"Frozen" means tomorrow's 900 labels are the same as today's, and you can prove it. There are four layers. Each one closes a gap the one before it leaves open.

  1. Pin the inputs. The same complaints table, the same rules table, the same settings. Record the row count so a silently changed table shows up.
  2. Pin the randomness. The seed on the train/test split (cell 2). Section 7 showed what happens without it.
  3. Record the evidence. Run cell 6 (fingerprint) and cell 13 (run log): date, rules and model versions, seed, row counts, fingerprint and library versions. Keep that row beside the labels.
  4. Pin the outcome. Copy cell 9's 900-row output and use Paste Special, Values onto a sheet called Frozen. The labels are now data rather than a calculation. They can't move when the workbook recalculates, when someone edits the model cell, or when a library update changes a borderline case.
Why layer 4 mattersLayers 1 to 3 make a recalculation reproducible on the same setup. Layer 4 makes the result permanent. If you only do layers 1 to 3 and the library versions change, a borderline label could still move. The fingerprint and run log are how you would notice.

Checking for drift

Put the frozen labels in the run_1 column of a table called Runs, and a fresh recalculation in run_2. Cell 14 reports the agreement and cell 15 lists any complaint that moved. 100% agreement means nothing has moved.

What freezing does not do

  • It doesn't make new complaints get the same labels as old ones. New data means a new run, so record it as a new version (for example tfidf-lr-v2) rather than overwriting the old one.
  • It doesn't make the labels correct. It makes them repeatable and explainable, so errors can be found and fixed deliberately.
Not tested in ExcelI tested the code in Python, not inside Excel. Paste Special, Values is ordinary Excel and shouldn't depend on Python, but check that it behaves as expected on a copy of your workbook first. In ordinary Python (outside Excel) the stronger version is to train once, save the model file, and only ever load it; the downloadable script does this.

10So what? The conclusion

What you did

  1. Loaded 900 complaints that already have the right category attached.
  2. Locked away 180 as an exam the model would never see, and taught it on the other 720.
  3. Measured it on the exam: 85.6% correct.
  4. Retrained it five times to check for hidden randomness. There was none.
  5. Labelled all 900 complaints with rules first, the model second, and a person for the rest, keeping the evidence for each label.
  6. Removed the seed to see what breaks, and lined the two 900-row outputs up side by side.

What it proves

  • A TF-IDF and logistic regression classifier is reproducible. The same data, settings and split give identical labels and probabilities every run.
  • The one random choice in the process is the train/test split. Pin it with a seed and results repeat; leave it out and results change every run, by 47 to 55 complaints out of 900 in these tests.
  • Reproducible is not the same as correct. It is right on 85.6% of unseen complaints and consistently wrong on the rest. Reproducibility just lets you measure that error and fix it deliberately.
  • Rules and the model fail in different ways. Rules are explainable but narrow; the model covers everything but can't show simple reasons.
  • The model's confidence is informative. On test complaints where it was at least 60% confident it was right 92.9% of the time (156 complaints). Below 60% it was right 37.5% (24 complaints). That gap is why a review queue is worth having.

What it does not prove

  • Nothing here shows how Copilot behaves. No LLM was run. The page shows the deterministic alternative, not that an LLM varies. Only a repeat-run test on your own complaints can measure that.
  • The accuracy figures are not your accuracy. The complaints are synthetic and tidy. Real data will score differently, so always measure on a labelled sample of your own.
  • It doesn't show the model beats rules in general. Only that it did on this data.

How this bears on your manager's claim

The claim was that five people running the same instructions on the same data would get exactly the same response. For the method on this page that is true, but only because every source of randomness can be pinned: the data, the settings and the split seed. Remove the seed and five people get five different answers (experiment B). For an LLM prompt there is no equivalent setting you control from inside the prompt, so the same guarantee isn't available, and Microsoft's own documentation says generative answers aren't deterministic.

The one-line versionWith a trained classifier, reproducibility is something you build by fixing the data and the seed. With an LLM prompt it is something you can only hope for and have to test.

11"Isn't this just a fuzzy scored lookup?"

A fair question, and the honest answer starts with "partly, yes". Here is exactly where the two are the same and where they differ.

The short versionBoth work the same way at the final step: look at the words in the complaint, add up points for each category, and pick the highest total. A scored keyword lookup and a TF-IDF classifier are close cousins. The difference is who writes the list of words and the points. In a lookup, a person writes them. In the classifier, the computer works them out by studying complaints that people have already labelled. After training, both are fixed tables that give the same answer every time.

An everyday way to see it

Scored lookupA sorting clerk with your cheat sheet
  • You write: "if you see fee, give Fees 2 points; if you see locked, give Account Access 3 points"
  • The clerk follows it to the letter
  • Anything not on the sheet scores nothing
Fuzzy lookupThe same clerk, a bit more forgiving
  • Still your cheat sheet
  • Now also accepts near-spellings: charged or chrage counts as charge
  • A word that isn't on the sheet in any spelling still scores nothing
Trained classifierA clerk who writes the cheat sheet himself
  • Reads 720 complaints that people have already labelled
  • Writes his own sheet of 819 words and word pairs, each with its own points
  • Then follows that sheet to the letter

Fuzzy matching helps with spelling. Training helps with vocabulary you didn't think to list. They solve different problems.

Side by side

Scored keyword lookup (exact or fuzzy)TF-IDF + logistic regression
Who writes the word listA person. Here: 59 keywords.The training step. Here: 819 words and word pairs.
Who sets the pointsA person's judgement ("fee = 2").Arithmetic on the labelled examples. A word that appears mostly in one category and rarely elsewhere earns more points for it.
Word pairsOnly if you write them out.Learns them automatically ("unexpected charge", "hold cut").
A word nobody thought to listScores nothing. Fuzzy matching only helps if it's a near-spelling of a listed word.Counts, if it appeared in the training complaints.
Common filler wordsIgnored unless you list them.Automatically down-weighted (the "TF-IDF" part of the name).
What you need to startDomain knowledge and time.A few hundred correctly labelled complaints. Poor labels give a poor model.
Explaining one labelEasy: "it contained these keywords".Possible but harder: "these learned words added up to the highest total". Some learned words look odd (see below).
Same answer every time?Yes, once the table is versioned.Yes, once the split seed is fixed and the model is frozen (sections 7 to 9).

One complaint, three methods

A held-out complaint that the model had never seen, picked as the first one in the test set where the exact keyword table found nothing and the strict fuzzy lookup (cell 17) also found nothing.

"My card reader stopped working and I cannot approve payments."
True label: Account Access
  • Exact keyword table: no keyword matched, so no label.
  • Fuzzy keyword lookup: no near-spelling of any listed keyword either, so no label.
  • Trained classifier: Account Access, 99% confident. These learned words did the work:
Word or word pair the model usedPoints toward Account Access
approve0.53
approve payments0.53
stopped0.53
stopped working0.53
reader0.53

The points shown are each word's TF-IDF value for this complaint multiplied by the weight the model learned for the predicted category. They are summed with an intercept and converted to a probability.

Does a fuzzy lookup close the gap? A real test

Cell 17 runs this on the 180 held-out complaints, with the same scoring rules as cell 3. Three ways of making the lookup more willing to answer are included, so the comparison is fair to the lookup.

answers (share of 180) accuracy when it answers overall accuracy (no answer = wrong)
Exact keywords (cell 3) 35.6% 82.8% 29.4%
Exact keywords, answer whenever any match 86.7% 73.7% 63.9%
Fuzzy keywords, strict (0.85) 36.7% 84.8% 31.1%
Fuzzy keywords, loose (0.75) 50.6% 76.9% 38.9%
TF-IDF + logistic regression 100.0% 85.6% 85.6%
  • Fuzzy spelling barely moves it. The strict version answers 36.7% instead of 35.6% of complaints. The words in the missing complaints weren't spelled wrongly. They simply weren't on the list.
  • Loosening the match answers more, but gets more wrong. Near-matches start catching words that merely look similar.
  • Making the exact lookup answer whenever any keyword matches gets to 86.7% coverage at 73.7% accuracy, still below the classifier's 85.6%.
Read this fairlyThe keyword table here is a 59-keyword first draft, and the data is synthetic. A person who keeps adding keywords would narrow this gap, and on real complaints the size of the gap could be larger or smaller. What the test does show is the direction: spelling tolerance isn't the missing ingredient. Coverage of vocabulary is, and that is what training supplies.

  • Sensible finds your table already had or could use: callback, misled, unexpected, card, stolen loan.
  • Words you might not have thought to list: error, arrived, included, safe, asked.
  • Junk: handled, account expect, badly age, account like. These came from boilerplate closing sentences in the synthetic data, which the model treated as evidence. A person reviewing this table would strike them out. A classifier will learn this kind of artefact from any real data that has repeated phrases, which is the main cost of the approach.

So what do you say?

A good reply to "do a fuzzy scored lookup then"
"That's a legitimate approach, and it's deterministic too. The two are close relatives: both add up word evidence. The difference is that a lookup only knows the words someone wrote down, while a trained classifier writes its own, much longer list from labelled examples. Fuzzy matching only fixes spelling, and on our test it hardly changed the result. Either approach gives the same answer every time once it's pinned, which was the point."
A practical middle route
"Train the model, read its highest-weighted words, strike out the junk, and keep the good ones as a human-approved keyword table. You get a lookup that is fully explainable and that started from evidence rather than guesswork. Compare it with the model on a held-out set before trusting it."
Avoid
"The classifier is just better." On a small, clean, well-understood problem a maintained lookup can be the better choice, because anyone can read and defend it. The classifier earns its place when wording is wider than anyone can list.

12The same three ideas using only Excel formulas

No Python, no add-ins, no Copilot. Ordinary formulas that work in any modern Excel, in a workbook you can download.

900 complaints, 59 keywords, 819 learned terms, every label a formula
How this was checkedI recalculated the workbook in LibreOffice and compared every label with the Python version. All three methods matched on all 900 complaints. I have not opened it in Excel itself. The functions used (SUMPRODUCT, SEARCH, INDEX, MATCH, LARGE, TRIM, SUBSTITUTE) are long-standing and need no dynamic arrays, but try it on your own copy first. The learned-weights sheet runs about 4 million text searches, so a full recalculation may take a few seconds.

1. Standard keyword scoring

Three things per complaint: clean the text, add up the weights of every keyword found (one column per category), then pick the winner only if it is strong and clearly ahead. The two thresholds sit in cells Rules!H1 and Rules!H2, so anyone can see and change them. Categories are listed in priority order, which makes MATCH break ties the same way every time.

Step 1: clean the text (column D). Lowercase it, turn punctuation into spaces, trim, and pad with a space at each end so that "fee" cannot match inside "feel".

=" "&TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(LOWER(B2),"."," "),","," "),"'"," "),"’"," "),"!"," "),"?"," "),";"," "),":"," "),"-"," "),"("," "),")"," "),"""", " "),"£"," "),"&"," "),"/"," "),"%"," "))&" "

Step 2: score one category (E2, filled across E to J and down). The pattern column in Rules is the keyword with a space either side.

=SUMPRODUCT((Rules!$A$2:$A$60=E$1)*Rules!$C$2:$C$60*ISNUMBER(SEARCH(Rules!$D$2:$D$60,$D2)))

Step 3: choose the label (K2).

=IF(OR(MAX(E2:J2)<Rules!$H$1,MAX(E2:J2)-LARGE(E2:J2,2)<Rules!$H$2),"No label",INDEX($E$1:$J$1,MATCH(MAX(E2:J2),E2:J2,0)))

2. Fuzzy keyword scoring, as far as formulas can take it

Excel has no built-in fuzzy matching function. What formulas can do is stem matching: match the start of a word, so a keyword like charge also catches charged, charges and charging. Only one formula changes. A second pattern column in Rules (E) trims the last two letters from single keywords of six letters or more, and the scoring formula points at it instead.

=IF(OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH(" ",B2)),LEN(B2)<6)," "&B2&" "," "&LEFT(B2,LEN(B2)-2))
=SUMPRODUCT((Rules!$A$2:$A$60=L$1)*Rules!$C$2:$C$60*ISNUMBER(SEARCH(Rules!$E$2:$E$60,$D2)))
  • What it handles: endings and word forms.
  • What it can't handle with formulas: typos such as chrage. That needs an edit-distance comparison. The options are Microsoft's separate Fuzzy Lookup add-in (which has to be installed, and which isn't the same thing as a formula), or the Python in Excel version in cell 17 of section 4.
  • The risk: stems also catch unwanted words. This is why I only stem keywords of six letters or more. Stemming a short keyword like app would match "approve" and "apple".

3. The model's learned weights, run as a lookup

This is the part that matters for the question of what training adds. The frozen TF-IDF + logistic regression model is a table: every word or word pair it learned, with one weight per category. Exported to a sheet called Terms (819 rows, 6 weight columns, plus an intercept row), the scoring is the same shape as the keyword scorer, with learned weights in place of hand-written ones.

=SUMPRODUCT(ISNUMBER(SEARCH(" "&Terms!$A$3:$A$821&" ",$D2))*Terms!B$3:B$821)+Terms!B$2
=INDEX($S$1:$X$1,MATCH(MAX(S2:X2),S2:X2,0))

This is an approximation of the Python model, not a copy. It matches words as they are written, while the Python model first removes common words and scales each complaint's word values. The two agree on 93.9% of the held-out complaints and on 92.2% of all 900. Training itself (working out the weights) still needs Python or another tool. Formulas only apply the finished table.

The results, side by side

On the 180 held-out complaints (the ones the model never saw). Use these rows for any comparison. On the 720 the model learned from, it scores 91.5%, which flatters it.

MethodAnswers (share)Accuracy when it answersOverall accuracy (no answer = wrong)
Exact keywords, formulas (section 12, part 1)35.6%82.8%29.4%
Stem-fuzzy keywords, formulas (part 2)42.2%78.9%33.3%
Learned weights as a lookup, formulas (part 3)100.0%85.6%85.6%
TF-IDF + logistic regression, Python (cell 4)100.0%85.6%85.6%

The keyword rows don't learn from data, so their figures are the same on the held-out complaints as on any other set, apart from my having written the keywords knowing roughly what the complaints look like.

Have we gone wrong? Is there a gap?

A fair challenge, so here is the straight answer. The result stands, but the story I told around it needed tightening.

What we might have impliedWhat the evidence supports
"Frozen TF-IDF with a seed has magic that keyword rules lack."The useful ingredient is a weighted word list built from labelled examples. Once built, it can run as formulas (above), at the same accuracy on the held-out set (85.6%). Nothing about it needs a clever algorithm at run time.
"The seed is what freezes it."The seed only decides which complaints are held back for testing. Training itself has no random step here (section 7, experiment C). What actually freezes the behaviour is the table of weights. If you save that table, the seed no longer matters for running it.
"Rules score 29.4%, the classifier 85.6%."Partly an artefact of a deliberately thin 59-keyword first draft that declines to answer most complaints. The fairer comparison is a lookup built from the same labelled data, and that is what the Terms sheet is. A person extending the keyword list for long enough would close much of the gap.
"Determinism is the classifier's advantage."Determinism belongs to any fixed table, written by a person or learned by a machine. It is the difference between those and an LLM prompt that this page is really about.
What the classifier genuinely addsIt builds and weights a far larger word list than a person would write (819 against 59), it picks up word pairs, and it does this in seconds from labelled examples. That saves labour and finds vocabulary nobody thought of. It also learns junk from repeated boilerplate, so the list needs a human read before anyone relies on it.
Limits of this whole comparisonThe data is synthetic. Complaints in the real world are messier, labels are less clean, and the gap in either direction could be bigger or smaller. This page shows what can be pinned and how a fixed table behaves. It doesn't measure Copilot.

What this means for the argument with Scott

Safe to say
"The thing that gives you the same answer every time is a fixed table of words and weights. You can write the table by hand, learn it from labelled examples, or do both. Either way it runs as ordinary formulas and gives the same label on every recalculation. An LLM prompt isn't a fixed table, and nothing in the documentation guarantees it behaves like one."
Avoid
"TF-IDF is the answer and keyword lookups can't compete." On this data a lookup built from labelled examples does well and a hand-written draft does badly, and that gap is about effort and coverage, not about magic.

13Why use Python at all, if formulas give the same accuracy?

A fair challenge, because section 12 shows a frozen model can run as plain formulas. This is the justification I can defend, and the part of it that doesn't hold.

Executive summary
  1. Python builds the table. It doesn't have to run it. It reads 720 labelled complaints and works out 819 weighted words and word pairs in seconds. A person can't realistically do that by hand.
  2. The fixed seed makes the test repeatable. It decides which 180 complaints are held back, so the same seed gives the same split and the same accuracy figure. It is bookkeeping, not a clever ingredient.
  3. Once built, the table is what gives the same answer every time. Run it in Python or in formulas.
  4. Python also gives you the evidence: confidence scores, a fair accuracy test, a fingerprint and a run log.

Where Python wins

ReasonWhat the evidence on this page shows
Only Python builds the weightsFormulas can apply the 819 learned weights but can't produce them. Without the training step the table doesn't exist, and you are back to writing keywords by hand.
"Same results" is true for accuracy, not for every labelThe formula version scores 85.6% on held-out complaints, the same as the Python model's 85.6%. But on those 180 complaints it gives a different label to the Python model on 11 of them (6.1%), and agrees on 93.9%. It skips the model's stop-word removal and length scaling. The Python model is the reference.
Only Python gives a confidence scoreThe hybrid process in cell 7 sends anything under 60% confidence to a person. The formula version has no calibrated confidence, so that safety net is lost.
Only Python gives the audit evidenceThe train and test split, precision and recall, the fingerprint (cell 6), the run log (cell 13) and the seed experiment (cell 10) all come from Python. Formulas have no clean equivalent.
ScaleThe formula workbook makes about 4.4 million text searches to label 900 complaints. At 25,000 complaints that is roughly 28 times more, about 123 million per recalculation. That is slow and fragile in a workbook.
RetrainingWhen new labelled complaints arrive, Python retrains and produces a new version with its own fingerprint. A formula table has to be re-exported from Python anyway.

Where Python doesn't win

  • Running a frozen table is no more deterministic in Python than in formulas. Both give the same label every time once the table is fixed.
  • Formulas can be easier to audit. Anyone can read a SUMPRODUCT and a sheet of weights without knowing Python.
  • So the claim to make is narrower: Python builds, tests and proves the table. It doesn't classify more reliably than a fixed table run any other way.

The one thing to check before you demo

Python in ExcelMicrosoft's page on open-source libraries lists scikit-learn among the libraries Python in Excel offers, and says those libraries can't make network requests or read files on your computer. That is why the cells here only use data inside the workbook. I have not run these cells inside Excel, and I haven't checked which scikit-learn version it provides. Try the cells on a copy of your workbook first. If something fails, the downloadable local script (section 3) does the same training in ordinary Python, and you can bring the finished table into Excel.
Microsoft: Open-source libraries and Python in Excel
Safe to say
"Python is how you build and prove the table. Once it's built, anything can run it, and Python's job is the build, the test and the evidence."
Avoid
"Only Python can do this." Formulas can run the finished table. What they can't do is build it.

14Making the case, including to a sceptic

What you can say accurately, the objections you will hear, and a fair way to settle it with evidence.

Safe to say
"Microsoft's Copilot Studio documentation lists, among the limitations of generative answers, that answers from language models aren't deterministic. So identical runs aren't guaranteed to match, and we can measure how much ours vary."
Safe to say
"A keyword table, or a trained classifier with a fixed split seed and the labels stored as values, gives the same result on every run, and we can prove it with a fingerprint."
Avoid
"Copilot is always inconsistent." Often it isn't. The accurate claim is that nothing guarantees it, and that has to be tested.Also avoid saying Microsoft states this about a specific product or task unless you have found that exact page.

Objections you will hear, and straight answers

"…"A fair answer
"I've tried it and it gives the same answer."Often it will, especially on clear-cut complaints. This page shows a similar pattern when the training split changes: a stable majority, with the movement on borderline cases. An LLM's variation comes from different causes, so that isn't proof of how Copilot behaves, but borderline complaints are the first place to look. Run the test below on your own data.
"We'll tell it to be consistent, with precise instructions."A closed list of categories, examples and strict output formats narrow the variation, but none removes it. A prompt can't set a seed, and I haven't found a documented seed setting for Copilot Studio agents.
"Python in Excel is Microsoft AI too."It runs ordinary code on Microsoft's servers; it isn't generative AI. Copilot can help write the code, and that part will vary. Once the code is written and pinned, it behaves the same way each time it runs. That is the difference between writing and running.
"Only about 3.6% changed. That's close enough."For some uses it is. For a complaints or redress process, a rate like that on 25,000 complaints is roughly 890 labels that could differ between two runs, and each needs an explanation if it is challenged. The aim isn't zero error. It is being able to reproduce and explain every label.
"Your demo isn't Copilot, so it proves nothing about Copilot."Correct, and this page says so. It shows what can be pinned in a classifier. Whether Copilot varies on your data is an empirical question, and the test below answers it using the same yardstick.
"We can just save Copilot's answers."Yes, and that is a legitimate way to freeze them: store the label, the prompt version and the date, and treat the stored label as the answer. The difference is that nobody can regenerate it later and expect the same label, and a stored label is only as defensible as that first run, so you would want a person to confirm it.
"Microsoft will fix this."Possibly. Nothing I found promises reproducible output from generative answers, so don't build a process around a guarantee that doesn't exist today.

Test Copilot yourself, with the same yardstick

This is a fair test, and it could come out in Copilot's favour. If it does, say so.

  1. Take the test kit. It holds all 900 complaints with the true label and the seeded model's confidence. Pick 100 rows: 50 with confidence under 80% (borderline) and 50 over 90% (clear-cut), so both ends are tested.
  2. Run your Copilot agent over those 100 complaints and record each label in run_1. Then run it again in a fresh session with identical instructions and record run_2. Don't ask for a confidence score and don't show it the true label.
  3. Load the kit as an Excel Table called Runs (alongside the Complaints table) and run cells 14 and 15. Only complaints with a label in both columns are compared.
  4. Read the answer. 100% agreement on your sample is real evidence in Copilot's favour for that sample and that day. Anything lower gives you a number to show instead of an argument. Repeat it after a Copilot or model update, because "the same on Tuesday" isn't "the same for ever".
